content.text: Some atomic nuclei are unstable and spontaneously emit particles and energy—a process called radioactive decay. Discovered by Henri Becquerel in 1896 and studied extensively by Marie Curie, radioactivity has applications from medicine to power generation, but also presents hazards that must be understood and managed.

Radioactive decay is both random (we cannot predict which nucleus will decay next) and spontaneous (it happens without any external trigger and is unaffected by temperature, pressure, or chemical conditions).

When measuring radioactivity in an experiment, always subtract the background count rate from your readings. Background radiation is always present and must be accounted for to get an accurate measurement of the source's activity.

Students often think that more penetrating means more dangerous. In fact, alpha radiation is the most dangerous if ingested or inhaled because it is the most strongly ionising. Gamma is more penetrating but less ionising per unit distance.

Radioactivity: spontaneous, random emission from unstable nuclei
Alpha (α): helium nucleus, +2 charge, stopped by paper, strongly ionising
Beta (β): electron, −1 charge, stopped by aluminium, moderately ionising
Gamma (γ): EM wave, no charge, reduced by thick lead, weakly ionising
Detection: Geiger-Müller tube, photographic film, cloud chamber
Background radiation: always present, mostly natural
Always correct for background when measuring sources
a) Alpha: 2 protons and 2 neutrons (a helium-4 nucleus). b) Beta: a high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus. c) Gamma: a high-energy electromagnetic wave (photon) with no mass or charge.
a) Penetrating ability: alpha (least), beta, gamma (most). b) Ionising ability: gamma (least), beta, alpha (most).
— penetration and ionisation are inversely related (comparison)

Alpha particles are large, heavy (+2 charge, mass 4), and strongly ionising, so they lose energy rapidly and are stopped by a few cm of air or paper. Gamma rays have no charge and no mass, interact weakly with matter, and pass through paper easily.
— high ionising ability leads to low penetration (reasoning)
